title: South Africa | Joint Standard on Cybersecurity, Operational Resilience and POPIA
tagline: Meet the PA and FSCA cyber Joint Standard, the 2026 incident template, the PA's resilience directive and POPIA's safeguard and breach rules.
sectors: South African banks, branches of foreign banks and mutual banks
Bank controlling companies and their groups
Contact centres and outsourced service partners
Bank IT, security operations and incident response
Privacy, compliance and operational risk teams
description:
A South Africa-specific cybersecurity, resilience and privacy quest for bank staff. It is based on **Joint Standard 2 of 2024 (Cybersecurity and Cyber Resilience Requirements)**, made by the **Prudential Authority** and the **Financial Sector Conduct Authority** under the Financial Sector Regulation Act and in force since 1 June 2025; **Joint Notice 2 of 2026**, which sets the template banks file on the PA's Umoja portal for material IT and cyber incidents from 1 September 2026; **Joint Standard 1 of 2023** on IT governance and risk; the PA's **Directive 4 of 2023** on operational resilience; and the **Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013 (POPIA)**, enforced by the **Information Regulator**.

Paragraph 7.2.7 of Joint Standard 2 requires every bank to run a comprehensive cyber awareness programme for all users, including contractors and third-party staff with system access, with refresher training at least once a year, regular new content, training for the board and periodic review of the programme. This quest is designed to support that duty for all staff, and gives managers, incident teams, privacy staff and directors the governance, incident notification and resilience knowledge their roles need.

It builds knowledge of the rules and real public cases; it does not replace your institution's own cyber, privacy, incident response and business continuity policies and procedures, which you must always follow.
audience: All employees of South African banks who use bank systems or handle customer information
Contractors, consultants and outsourced staff with access to a bank's systems or information
IT, security operations and incident response teams
Information officers, deputy information officers and privacy and compliance teams
Senior managers and board members who oversee cyber risk and operational resilience
outcomes: Explain who made Joint Standards 1 and 2, when they apply and what the board and management must put in place
Apply the paragraph 7.2.7 training duty, including who counts as a user and how often refreshers happen
Recognise and report phishing, smishing, vishing and impersonation scams, and explain the hygiene controls behind every user
Apply POPIA's eight conditions, the section 19 safeguard duty and the operator rules to everyday banking tasks
Classify incidents and meet the Joint Notice 2 of 2026 timelines and POPIA section 22 notification duties
Explain Directive 4 of 2023 on operational resilience and prepare evidence for a supervisory review

quest.name: The Resilience Mandate
quest.premise: You have just joined the information security office of Marula Bank Limited, a fictional South African bank with its head office in Rosebank, Johannesburg, a security operations centre in Midrand, a hub in Durban and a contact centre in Gqeberha. The Prudential Authority has scheduled a review of how the bank meets the cyber Joint Standard. With CISO Lindiwe Khumalo, incident lead Johan Botha, information officer Fatima Essop, contact centre lead Kagiso Molefe and board committee chair Zanele Nkosi, clear five stages, then face the final review.

sessions.title: The Joint Standards: Governance, Scope and the Training Duty
sessions.summary: Who makes South Africa's bank cyber rules, which institutions they cover, what Joint Standard 2 of 2024 asks the board and management to build, and the paragraph 7.2.7 awareness training duty.
objectives: Explain the roles of the Prudential Authority and the FSCA in making the Joint Standards
State when Joint Standards 1 and 2 took effect and which institutions they cover
Describe the board's ultimate responsibility and the governance structure the cyber standard expects
Apply paragraph 7.2.7: who must be trained, how often, and how the programme is kept current

cards.title: Day one: the Standards Room
cards.setting: Information security office, Marula Bank head office, Rosebank, Johannesburg. A Monday in November 2026.

lines.text: Your access badge works, but your laptop refuses to open email until you approve a sign-in on your phone. A note on the desk reads: 'Welcome to the cyber team. Coffee at nine. Lindiwe.'
Morning! I'm Lindiwe Khumalo, the bank's CISO. You picked a lively time to join. The Prudential Authority wants to walk through how we meet the cyber Joint Standard next month.
Johan Botha, incident response, out of the Midrand security operations centre. And since September we also report material incidents on the new template. No more improvising.
Kagiso Molefe, contact centre in Gqeberha. Half my agents work for an outsourcer. Does this cyber standard even touch them?
Fatima Essop, information officer. And remember POPIA sits right next to all of this. When customer data is involved, the Information Regulator cares too.
Five stages, one mission: show the regulators that every person here knows the rules and their part in them. Stage one is the rulebook itself. Let's open it.

cards.title: Who writes South Africa's bank cyber rules

scenes.heading: Twin peaks
scenes.narration: South Africa splits financial regulation between two authorities. The Prudential Authority, inside the Reserve Bank, keeps banks safe and sound. The Financial Sector Conduct Authority watches how they treat customers.

scenes.heading: Joint Standards
scenes.narration: Under the Financial Sector Regulation Act, the two authorities can make binding standards together. For technology they made two: Joint Standard 1 of 2023 on IT governance and risk, and Joint Standard 2 of 2024 on cybersecurity and cyber resilience.

scenes.heading: When they bite
scenes.narration: Joint Standard 1 has applied since 15 November 2024. Joint Standard 2 was published in May 2024 and has applied since 1 June 2025, giving firms about a year to prepare.

scenes.heading: Who is covered
scenes.narration: The cyber standard covers banks, branches of foreign banks, controlling companies and mutual banks, along with insurers, fund managers, market infrastructures and others. A bank or controlling company must also cover cyber risk in the entities structured under it.

scenes.heading: Proportionate, not optional
scenes.narration: The standard expects a bank to apply its minimum requirements in a way that fits its size, complexity and risk profile. Proportionality changes how you comply, never whether you comply.

cards.title: The South African cyber and resilience rulebook
cards.caption: Dates as stated in the PA and FSCA documents. Always check the authorities' websites for later changes.

items.label: Directive 4 of 2023
items.detail: The PA directs banks to apply the Basel operational resilience principles.

items.label: Joint Standard 1 published
items.detail: IT governance and risk management requirements for financial institutions.

items.label: Joint Standard 2 published
items.detail: Cybersecurity and cyber resilience requirements, made jointly by the PA and FSCA.

items.label: Joint Standard 1 in force
items.detail: IT strategy, IT risk framework, IT resilience and incident notification apply.

items.label: Resilience deadline
items.detail: Banks had to meet Directive 4 of 2023 by this date.

items.label: Joint Standard 2 in force
items.detail: Cyber governance, controls, training and notification duties apply.

items.label: Joint Notice 2 of 2026
items.detail: A set template for notifying material IT and cyber incidents takes effect.

cards.question: Who made Joint Standard 2 of 2024 on cybersecurity and cyber resilience?
options: The Information Regulator under POPIA
The Prudential Authority and the FSCA together, under the FSR Act
The Financial Intelligence Centre under the FIC Act
The Banking Association as an industry code
cards.explanation: It is a joint standard: the Prudential Authority and the Financial Sector Conduct Authority made it together under the Financial Sector Regulation Act. POPIA is a separate law enforced by the Information Regulator.

cards.title: Who carries cyber accountability at Marula Bank
cards.caption: Joint Standard 2 places final responsibility at the top, but the controls only work if every layer plays its part.

items.label: Governing body (the board)
items.detail: Ultimately responsible for compliance and cyber risk oversight; approves the cyber strategy and framework.

items.label: Board committee
items.detail: May carry the primary oversight work the board delegates, such as an IT and risk committee.

items.label: Senior management
items.detail: Builds and runs the strategy and framework with the board; reports risk metrics.

items.label: Cyber and information security function
items.detail: Properly resourced, with authority and access to the board, and separated from conflicts.

items.label: Every user
items.detail: Staff, contractors, consultants and providers with system access: follow policy and report.

cards.title: What Joint Standard 2 asks a bank to build
cards.body:
Think of the standard as a set of building blocks the bank must have, approved and kept current:

- **Strategy and framework:** a board-approved cybersecurity strategy, reviewed at least once a year, and a cyber framework aligned with enterprise risk management and reviewed at least yearly through an independent review.
- **Identify:** know your critical processes and information assets, classify them by criticality and sensitivity, and keep an asset inventory that is reviewed at least every two years.
- **Protect:** access control, data security, secure systems and networks, cryptography and **awareness training**.
- **Detect, respond and recover:** monitoring, an incident response plan, backups and customer communication.
- **Situational awareness, testing and learning:** threat intelligence, testing, remediation and lessons learnt.
- **Hygiene:** strong access management, multi-factor authentication, patching, secure configuration and malware protection.
- **Notification:** tell the responsible authority when an incident is classified as material.

cards.title: Cyber standard or IT governance standard?
cards.prompt: Sort each duty into the Joint Standard that mainly carries it.

items.text: Cyber awareness refresher training for all users at least yearly
An IT strategy approved by the board and reviewed at least yearly
Multi-factor authentication for privileged and administrative accounts
An IT risk management framework covering all material IT risks
Penetration testing of systems reachable from the internet
Notifying a material systems failure, malfunction or delay
Taking part in trusted cyber threat information sharing
Managing IT programmes and projects in a controlled way

cards.title: The question from the boardroom
cards.setting: Video call between Rosebank, Gqeberha and the board office. Late afternoon.

lines.text: Zanele Nkosi here, chair of the board's IT and risk committee. Lindiwe, the PA letter asks what training the board itself has had. Is that really their business?
It is. The cyber standard says the governing body must be trained so it understands technology risk and how cyber risk is managed. It's not just for staff.
And my outsourced agents? HR says the annual course is only for Marula employees.
Look at how the standard defines a user: employees, contractors, consultants and third-party providers who can get into our systems or information. If they log into our CRM, they're users.
Then let's get this right before the PA asks. Show me the options.

cards.title: Forty agents, one login each
cards.situation: Marula's outsourced contact centre partner in Gqeberha supplies 40 agents. Each has a Marula login to the customer relationship system and can see account details. HR plans to run the yearly cyber awareness refresher only for permanent Marula staff, saying the partner 'handles its own training'. Kagiso asks you what to do.

choices.text: Agree with HR. The agents are not Marula employees, so Marula's training duty does not reach them.
choices.outcome: Risky. Joint Standard 2 counts contractors and third-party service providers with access to the bank's systems as users. Leaving them out creates a gap in the bank's own awareness programme that a supervisor can easily spot.

choices.text: Bring the agents into Marula's awareness programme, or make sure by contract and evidence that the partner's training meets Marula's programme, and track completion for every login.
choices.outcome: Best answer. The bank must keep a high level of awareness among all users. It can deliver the training itself or rely on the partner, but it must be able to show that every person with access is covered and refreshed at least yearly.

choices.text: Send the agents a link to the cyber policy and ask them to read it when they have time.
choices.outcome: Better than nothing, but a policy link is not a comprehensive awareness programme, and there is no proof of completion or yearly refresher. The gap remains.

choices.text: Remove the agents' access to the CRM until the partner proves it trains its people.
choices.outcome: Too blunt. It would stop customer service without fixing the training gap. The right fix is to cover the agents in the programme and evidence it, not to break the service.

cards.title: Paragraph 7.2.7: the training duty in plain words
cards.caption: Joint Standard 2 of 2024, paragraph 7.2.7, summarised in our own words.

items.label: All users
items.right: Keep a high level of cyber awareness across everyone with access

items.label: Refreshers
items.right: Every user repeats the core training yearly or more often

items.label: New content
items.right: Add material as threats change, not only at the yearly refresher

items.label: Governing body
items.right: Understand technology risk and cyber risk management practice

items.label: The programme
items.right: Update for policy changes, emerging risks and the threat landscape

cards.back: Anything observable happening in an IT system. Many events are harmless; some signal an incident.
An event that threatens the security of a system or its information, or breaks security or acceptable use policy, whether malicious or not.
A disruption with, or likely to have, a severe and widespread impact on the bank's operations, its customers or the wider financial system.
Employees, contractors, consultants and third-party providers who have access to the bank's IT systems or information assets.
The ability to keep delivering the mission by anticipating and adapting to threats, and withstanding, containing and quickly recovering from incidents.
Several layers of people, process and technology controls, so that if one fails another limits the damage.

cards.question: Under paragraph 7.2.7, how often must user refresher training on cybersecurity happen at a minimum?
options: Every two years, in line with the asset inventory review
Only when a new employee joins
At least once a year, with new content added regularly
Only after a material incident
cards.explanation: The standard requires refresher training for users at least annually, plus regular training on new content as risks evolve. The two-year cycle belongs to the asset inventory review, not to training.

cards.title: Real case: the Justice department ransomware attack, 2021
cards.body:
On the evening of 6 September 2021 South Africa's Department of Justice and Constitutional Development was hit by ransomware. In its own public statement the department said all its information systems were encrypted and unavailable, affecting services such as letters of authority, bail services, email and its website.

The same statement explained that ransomware often spreads through **phishing emails with malicious attachments** or through **drive-by downloads**, where simply visiting an infected website installs malware.

**Why it matters for training:** the department's description of the entry routes points straight at everyday user behaviour. Opening an attachment or clicking a link can start an attack that stops a whole organisation. This is exactly why Joint Standard 2 makes awareness training a duty for *all* users, refreshed at least yearly, and not a nice-to-have for the IT team.

*Source: Department of Justice and Constitutional Development statement on gov.za, September 2021.*

cards.title: Stage 1 take-aways
items: Joint Standard 2 of 2024 (cyber) applies to banks from 1 June 2025; Joint Standard 1 of 2023 (IT governance) from 15 November 2024.
Both were made jointly by the Prudential Authority and the FSCA under the Financial Sector Regulation Act.
The board is ultimately responsible for cyber compliance and oversight, and approves the cyber strategy and framework.
Paragraph 7.2.7: awareness programme for all users, refreshers at least yearly, new content regularly, board training and periodic programme review.
Contractors and third-party providers with system access are users too.

cards.prompt: Think about who can log into the systems you use every day. Are there contractors, consultants or partner staff among them, and how would you check that they are covered by your bank's cyber awareness programme?

quiz.question: Since when has Joint Standard 2 of 2024 on cybersecurity and cyber resilience applied to South African banks?
options: 15 November 2024
31 December 2024
1 September 2026
1 June 2025
quiz.explanation: The authorities confirmed 1 June 2025 as the effective date of Joint Standard 2. 15 November 2024 is the date for Joint Standard 1, and 1 September 2026 is when the incident template took effect.

quiz.question: Marula Bank's outsourced contact centre agents log into the bank's CRM. How does Joint Standard 2 treat them for awareness training?
options: As outsiders, so only their employer's rules apply
As users only if they hold a bank employment contract
As users, so the bank's programme must cover them
As exempt, because they are covered by POPIA instead
quiz.explanation: The standard defines users to include contractors and third-party service providers with access to the bank's systems or information assets. The bank must be able to show they are covered.

quiz.question: Which body is ultimately responsible for a bank's compliance with Joint Standard 2?
options: The chief information security officer
The external auditor
The Prudential Authority's supervision team
The governing body (board of directors)
quiz.explanation: The standard places ultimate responsibility on the governing body, which may delegate primary oversight work to a committee but keeps the accountability.

quiz.question: The board of a mid-sized bank asks whether it must undergo any cyber training itself. What does paragraph 7.2.7 say?
options: Board members are exempt because they do not use bank systems
Only the chair of the risk committee must be trained
Board training is optional if the CISO reports every quarter
The governing body must be trained on technology risk and cyber risk management
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 7.2.7 expressly requires the governing body to undergo training that raises its awareness of technology risk and improves its understanding of cyber risk management practice.

quiz.question: How often must a bank's cybersecurity strategy be reviewed under Joint Standard 2?
options: Only when the board changes
Regularly, and at least once a year
Every three years with the audit plan
Only after a material incident
quiz.explanation: The standard requires the strategy to be reviewed regularly but at least annually to reflect the threat landscape, resources, gaps and lessons learnt.

quiz.question: A small mutual bank argues that because it is small, Joint Standard 2 does not apply to it. What is the best response?
options: It applies, but the bank may implement it in a way that fits its size and risk
It is correct: the standard covers only large banks
It applies only if the bank uses cloud services
It applies only after the PA grants written approval
quiz.explanation: Mutual banks are listed as financial institutions under the standard. Proportionality affects how the requirements are implemented, not whether they apply.

quiz.question: Which of these is a Joint Standard 2 requirement about the training programme itself?
options: It must be approved by the Information Regulator
It must be delivered only in a classroom
It must be reviewed periodically to keep its content current
It must be identical for every financial institution
quiz.explanation: The programme must be reviewed periodically, taking into account changes in security policy, emerging risks and the evolving threat landscape.

quiz.question: A staff member installs an unapproved file-sharing app and uploads a customer list by mistake, with no malicious intent. Under the standard's definitions, is this a cyber incident?
options: No, because no attacker was involved
No, because only events affecting availability count
Yes, because breaking security or acceptable use policy counts even without malice
Only if the Information Regulator says so
quiz.explanation: The standard defines a cyber incident to include events that violate security policies or acceptable use policies, whether or not they result from malicious activity.

quiz.question: A bank is a controlling company with subsidiaries in two other African countries. What does Joint Standard 2 expect regarding those subsidiaries?
options: They are ignored because they are licensed abroad
Their cyber risks must be catered for and mitigated in applying the standard
They must each apply for a separate South African licence
They are covered only if they share the same IT system
quiz.explanation: For banks and controlling companies, the standard requires cyber risks from juristic persons and branches structured under them, local and foreign, to be catered for and mitigated.

quiz.question: Which statement correctly compares the two Joint Standards?
options: Joint Standard 1 covers POPIA; Joint Standard 2 covers anti-money laundering
Both cover only insurers and pension funds
Joint Standard 1 covers IT governance and risk; Joint Standard 2 covers cybersecurity and cyber resilience
Joint Standard 2 replaced Joint Standard 1 on 1 June 2025
quiz.explanation: Joint Standard 1 of 2023 sets IT governance and risk management requirements; Joint Standard 2 of 2024 sets cyber requirements. They operate side by side; neither replaced the other.

sessions.title: Phishing, Social Engineering and Access Hygiene
sessions.summary: How criminals talk their way into banks through email, SMS, calls and messaging, how to spot, stop and report a lure, and the access and malware controls Joint Standard 2 requires behind every user.
objectives: Recognise phishing, smishing, vishing, spoofing and advance-fee lures and their warning signs
Respond correctly when you receive or fall for a lure, including prompt reporting
Describe the Joint Standard 2 hygiene controls on MFA, least privilege, privileged access and malware
Use the SARB's public warning on scams that abuse its name to verify regulator contact

cards.title: A call from 'the Reserve Bank'
cards.setting: Marula Bank contact centre, Gqeberha. Tuesday, 10:40.

lines.text: We had a strange one this morning. A caller said he was from the Reserve Bank's compliance division and needed a customer's account details to 'release a frozen foreign transfer'.
And at Midrand we caught an email to the payments team: the PA's logo, a link to 'confirm your Umoja login'. The sender domain was one letter off.
Same playbook, two channels. Authority, urgency and a request for something only we can give: data, credentials or a payment.
My agent refused and logged it. But she says she nearly believed him. He knew the customer's name and branch.
That's why stage two matters. Criminals rarely break in through the firewall. They talk their way in. Welcome to the Lure Line.

scenes.heading: The pretext
scenes.narration: The attacker borrows a trusted identity: a regulator, a senior executive, a supplier, IT support or a customer. A logo or a known name makes the story feel real.

scenes.heading: Pressure
scenes.narration: Next comes urgency or fear. 'Your account will be frozen today.' 'The CEO needs this payment before the meeting.' Pressure is designed to stop you from checking.

scenes.heading: Secrecy
scenes.narration: Many lures ask you to keep it confidential or to skip the usual process. A request to bypass a control is itself a warning sign.

scenes.heading: The ask
scenes.narration: Finally, the real goal: a password or one-time PIN, customer data, a changed bank account, a payment, or a click that installs malware.

scenes.heading: Many channels
scenes.narration: The same tricks arrive by email (phishing), SMS (smishing), voice calls (vishing), WhatsApp, social media or even a letter. Defend the person, not just the inbox.

cards.title: From lure to loss
cards.caption: Every stage is a chance to stop the attack. The earlier someone pauses and checks, the cheaper the stop.

items.label: Wide net
items.detail: Thousands of messages or calls go out, often using public details and stolen data.

items.label: Hook
items.detail: A few people respond to a believable story with a trusted name or logo.

items.label: Trust built
items.detail: The attacker adds detail, urgency and secrecy to keep the target engaged.

items.label: The ask
items.detail: Credentials, a one-time PIN, customer data, a payment or a malicious click.

items.label: Loss
items.detail: Account takeover, data breach, fraud or ransomware across the bank.

cards.question: An email shows the Prudential Authority's logo and asks you to 'urgently confirm your Umoja portal password' through a link. What is the strongest warning sign?
options: It mentions a real portal
It asks you to give your password through a link under time pressure
It was sent on a weekday
It has a logo
cards.explanation: Logos and real names are easy to copy. A request for credentials through a link, combined with urgency, is the classic phishing pattern. Check through a channel you already trust.

cards.title: Name the lure
cards.prompt: Match each attack to its description.

pairs.right: A deceptive email that tries to get you to click, open an attachment or give credentials
The same trick sent by SMS, often with a short link and an urgent warning
A phone call where the caller pretends to be a bank, regulator or IT support
Forging the sender so a message seems to come from a trusted address
Malware installed just by visiting an infected or malicious website
A promise of a large sum in return for fees or details paid up front

cards.title: Hygiene controls in Joint Standard 2 that blunt the lure
cards.body:
Training is one layer. Joint Standard 2 also requires technical and process controls that limit what a fooled user can damage:

- **Multi-factor authentication:** for users with access to critical system functions; MFA or privileged access management for all administrative and privileged accounts; and MFA for every account that reaches applications holding sensitive information over the internet.
- **Least privilege and segregation of duties:** access is granted according to role, with periodic access reviews by system and asset owners.
- **Privileged accounts:** granted on a need-to-use basis, logged and reviewed.
- **Remote access:** only from secured devices or connections, with strong authentication.
- **Malware protection:** endpoint protection that covers malicious links, websites, email attachments and infected removable media.
- **Browsing and cloud services:** internet browsing separated from sensitive systems, and controls against unauthorised internet services used to share or store sensitive data.

cards.title: Red flag or routine?
cards.prompt: Sort each situation at Marula Bank.

items.text: A 'supplier' emails new bank details and asks you to update them before today's payment run
A caller says he is from the Reserve Bank and needs a customer's account details
Your sign-in asks for MFA when you log in from home through the bank's secure connection
An SMS asks you to read back the one-time PIN you just received to 'IT support'
Your manager asks you in the team meeting to complete the yearly cyber refresher
A WhatsApp from the 'CEO' asks you to buy vouchers and keep it secret
IT announces a planned patch window through the usual intranet notice
A USB stick labelled 'Salaries 2026' is left in the staff kitchen

cards.title: He knew the customer's name
cards.setting: Contact centre floor, Gqeberha. Same afternoon.

lines.text: Here's what bothers me. The caller knew the customer's full name and branch. My agent said that made him sound official.
Names and branches leak all the time: social media, old breaches, even a customer's own posts. Knowing a detail proves nothing about who is calling.
And the Reserve Bank does not phone our agents asking for customer account details. If a regulator needs information, it comes through formal channels to compliance.
Let's practise. Same caller, but this time he's pushier.

cards.title: The pushy 'regulator'
cards.situation: A caller tells your agent he is from the South African Reserve Bank. He says a customer's incoming foreign transfer is being held and that he needs the customer's ID number, account number and recent balance within ten minutes, or 'the funds will be returned'. He gives a mobile number for call-backs and asks the agent not to involve a supervisor because 'this is confidential'.

choices.text: Give the details because the caller named the Reserve Bank and the customer could lose money.
choices.outcome: This is the scam succeeding. The pressure, secrecy and request for customer data are the lure. Disclosing it could breach POPIA and expose the customer to fraud.

choices.text: Politely decline, end the call, report it at once through the bank's phishing and fraud reporting route, and let compliance verify through official channels.
choices.outcome: Best answer. The agent protects customer data, does not use the caller's number, and gives the security and fraud teams what they need to warn others and look for related attempts.

choices.text: Call back the mobile number the caller gave to check he is genuine.
choices.outcome: A call-back only works on a number you already trust from an official source. The caller's own number will reach the caller. Report it instead.

choices.text: Give only the account number, since the ID number is more sensitive.
choices.outcome: Any customer data shared with an unverified caller is a disclosure risk, and an account number is valuable to fraudsters. Partial compliance still helps the attacker.

cards.title: Real case: the Reserve Bank's name used in '419' scams
cards.body:
The South African Reserve Bank warns on its own website that its corporate identity has been abused by syndicates running advance-fee ('419') scams. Victims receive letters, emails, SMSs, WhatsApp messages or social media messages showing the SARB logo or the names of SARB employees.

The pattern the SARB describes is classic social engineering: a promise of a large sum, a demand for **confidentiality**, then requests for **banking details, passport and identity documents**, followed by fees for fake lawyers or 'legal costs' until the victim stops paying.

The SARB points out that it does **not** hold bank accounts for private individuals or businesses and does **not** receive or hold cross-border transfers for members of the public. Victims are told to report to the South African Police Service and to the SARB's Financial Surveillance Department.

**Lesson for bank staff:** a regulator's name and logo are free to copy. Verify through official channels, never through contact details the sender supplies.

*Source: SARB 'Fraud and Scams' page, resbank.co.za.*

items.label: Spot
items.detail: Look for pressure, secrecy, odd senders, unusual requests and requests to bypass process.

items.label: Stop
items.detail: Do not click, reply, pay or share. End the call politely.

items.label: Verify
items.detail: Check through a channel you already trust: the intranet directory or official website.

items.label: Report
items.detail: Use the bank's phishing button or fraud and security reporting route at once.

items.label: Preserve
items.detail: Keep the email or call notes; do not forward the lure to colleagues.

cards.title: You clicked. Now what?
cards.prompt: You clicked a link in an email that now looks suspicious and typed your password. Put the right actions in order.
steps: Stop: do not enter anything else and close the page
Report immediately through the bank's security reporting route, saying what you clicked and entered
Change your password from a trusted device or follow the security team's reset instructions
Follow the security team's instructions, such as disconnecting the device if asked
Watch for unexpected MFA prompts and report any you did not start

cards.question: Which Joint Standard 2 requirement most directly limits the damage when an attacker steals an ordinary user's password for an internet-facing app holding sensitive data?
options: Yearly review of firewall rules
MFA for accounts that reach applications with sensitive information over the internet
A biennial review of the asset inventory
Board approval of the cyber strategy
cards.explanation: With MFA, a stolen password alone is not enough to log in. Joint Standard 2 requires MFA for all user accounts used to access applications containing sensitive information through the internet.

cards.title: Never share a one-time PIN
cards.body: No genuine colleague, IT support desk, bank or regulator needs your one-time PIN or password. If a caller asks for it, or you get MFA prompts you did not start, deny the prompt and report it straight away. Approving an unexpected prompt to 'make it stop' is how many account takeovers succeed.

cards.title: Stage 2 take-aways
items: Social engineering uses a trusted identity, pressure and secrecy to get credentials, data, payments or clicks.
It arrives by email, SMS, voice, WhatsApp, social media or letter: verify through channels you already trust.
Joint Standard 2 adds MFA, least privilege, privileged access control, malware protection and secure remote access.
The SARB warns that its name is abused in advance-fee scams and that it does not hold accounts or transfers for the public.
If you click or disclose, report immediately. Speed limits the damage.

cards.prompt: Recall a message or call you received that tried to rush you. Which warning signs were there, and what would you now do differently at each step of spot, stop, verify and report?

quiz.question: A caller claiming to be from the SARB asks a branch agent for a customer's account balance to 'release a foreign transfer'. Based on the SARB's public warning, what should the agent know?
options: The SARB does not hold accounts or cross-border transfers for the public
The SARB routinely calls bank agents for customer data
The request is valid if the caller knows the customer's name
Such requests must be answered within ten minutes
quiz.explanation: The SARB states that it does not keep accounts for private individuals or businesses and does not receive cross-border funds for members of the public. The call is a lure.

quiz.question: What is smishing?
options: Phishing carried out by voice calls
Malware hidden in a USB stick
A forged website that copies a bank's login page
Phishing carried out by SMS text message
quiz.explanation: Smishing uses SMS messages, often with a short link and an urgent warning. Vishing uses voice calls.

quiz.question: Under Joint Standard 2, which accounts must have MFA or at least privileged access management mechanisms?
options: All administrative and privileged accounts
Only accounts of board members
Only accounts created in the last year
Only customer-facing mobile banking accounts
quiz.explanation: The standard requires MFA, or at least privileged access management mechanisms, for all administrative and privileged accounts.

quiz.question: A supplier emails new banking details and asks the accounts team to update them before today's payment run. What is the best response?
options: Update the details because the email uses the supplier's logo
Verify the change with the supplier through contact details already on file before acting
Reply to the email asking if it is genuine
Pay half to the old account and half to the new one
quiz.explanation: Changed bank details under time pressure is a classic payment fraud pattern. Verify through a trusted channel, not by replying to the email.

quiz.question: Which control does Joint Standard 2 require to address malware delivered through malicious links, websites, email attachments and removable media?
options: A yearly penetration test of internal systems only
Board approval of every email attachment
Endpoint protection with up-to-date signatures and regular scanning
Disabling all internet access for all staff
quiz.explanation: The standard requires endpoint protection that addresses common malware delivery channels, up-to-date signatures, regular scanning and detection and response for indicators of compromise.

quiz.question: You receive several MFA prompts on your phone that you did not start. What should you do?
options: Approve one so the prompts stop
Ignore them and carry on working
Deny them and report to the security team straight away
Turn off MFA on your account
quiz.explanation: Unexpected prompts often mean someone has your password. Denying and reporting lets the security team reset credentials and investigate.

quiz.question: Which principle does Joint Standard 2 require when granting user access to systems?
options: Equal access for all staff to avoid complaints
Access for life once granted
Least privilege and segregation of duties, based on the user's role
Access decided by the user's own manager only, with no reviews
quiz.explanation: Access must follow segregation of duties and least privilege according to roles and responsibilities, with periodic user access reviews by system and asset owners.

quiz.question: A message tells you to keep a payment request confidential and not to involve your supervisor. Why is this a strong warning sign?
options: Confidential requests are always from the CEO
It asks you to bypass a normal control that would expose the fraud
Supervisors are not allowed to see payments
It proves the request comes from a regulator
quiz.explanation: Attackers ask for secrecy so that nobody checks. Any request to skip a normal control should be stopped and verified.

quiz.question: A contractor working for Marula Bank's IT supplier has access to production servers. How must the bank treat the contractor's access under Joint Standard 2?
options: Leave it to the supplier to monitor
Give it permanent administrator rights to save time
Subject it to the same monitoring and access restrictions as employees
Exclude it from access reviews because the person is not staff
quiz.explanation: The standard requires third-party providers and contractors with access to be subject to the same monitoring and access restrictions as the bank's own employees.

quiz.question: In its public statement on the 2021 ransomware attack, how did the Justice department say ransomware often spreads?
options: Through phishing emails with malicious attachments or drive-by downloads
Only through stolen laptops
Only through attacks on payment cards
Through faulty electricity supply
quiz.explanation: The department's statement explained that ransomware often spreads through phishing emails containing malicious attachments, or drive-by downloads from infected websites.

sessions.title: POPIA: Lawful Processing and Security Safeguards
sessions.summary: POPIA from the Act itself: the eight conditions for lawful processing, valid grounds, purpose and retention, the section 19 safeguard duty, operators under sections 20 and 21, special personal information, the information officer and the consequences of failure.
objectives: Name POPIA's eight conditions for lawful processing and apply them to banking situations
Identify a valid ground for processing and apply minimality, purpose and retention rules
Apply the section 19 safeguard cycle and the operator rules in sections 20 and 21
Explain the information officer's role and the main civil, administrative and criminal consequences

cards.title: Two requests before lunch
cards.setting: Privacy office, Marula Bank head office, Rosebank. Wednesday morning.

lines.text: Two emails this morning. Marketing wants to use ID copies and income data from account opening to target a new credit card. And a branch reports a stolen laptop with a spreadsheet of loan applicants.
The laptop is encrypted, so that one may be contained. But tell our new colleague why you look worried about the marketing request too.
Because POPIA isn't only about hackers. It's about whether we may use information at all, for what, and for how long. A breach is just one way to fail.
My agents hear 'POPIA' and think it means 'never say anything to anyone'. That can't be right either.
It isn't. POPIA lets us use personal information for good reasons, carefully. Stage three: the Privacy Vault. Let's learn the eight conditions.

scenes.heading: The Act
scenes.narration: The Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013, known as POPIA, sets the conditions for processing personal information in South Africa. The Information Regulator enforces it.

scenes.heading: Whose information
scenes.narration: Personal information means information about an identifiable, living person and, where it applies, an identifiable existing company or other juristic person. Think ID numbers, contact details, account and financial history.

scenes.heading: Responsible party
scenes.narration: The bank decides why and how customer information is processed, so it is the responsible party. It must make sure the conditions are met when it designs the processing and while it runs.

scenes.heading: Operators
scenes.narration: An operator processes information for the bank under a contract or mandate, such as a card processor, cloud provider or archiving firm. The bank stays accountable for what its operators do.

scenes.heading: The information officer
scenes.narration: Every body has an information officer who encourages and ensures compliance, deals with requests and works with the Regulator. The officer must be registered with the Regulator before taking up the role.

cards.title: The eight conditions for lawful processing (POPIA s 4)

cards.back: The responsible party makes sure every condition is met, both when it plans the processing and while it does it.
Process lawfully and reasonably, only what is adequate and relevant, on a valid ground, and usually collect from the person directly.
Collect for a specific, explicit and lawful purpose, and keep records no longer than needed unless an exception applies.
Any later use must be compatible with the original purpose of collection.
Take reasonable steps to keep information complete, accurate, not misleading and updated where needed.
Keep documentation of processing and tell people what is collected, by whom and why.
Protect integrity and confidentiality, control operators and notify compromises.
People may ask what is held about them and ask for corrections or deletion.

cards.question: Which POPIA condition contains section 19, the duty to secure personal information, and section 22, the duty to notify compromises?
options: Openness
Security safeguards
Information quality
Data subject participation
cards.explanation: Security safeguards is the seventh condition and covers sections 19 to 22: security measures, operators and notification of security compromises.

cards.title: Section 19: the safeguard cycle
cards.caption: POPIA expects appropriate, reasonable measures against loss, damage, unauthorised destruction and unlawful access or processing.

items.label: Identify risks
items.detail: Find all reasonably foreseeable internal and external risks to the personal information you hold or control.

items.label: Build safeguards
items.detail: Set up and maintain appropriate technical and organisational safeguards against those risks.

items.label: Verify
items.detail: Check regularly that the safeguards actually work as intended.

items.label: Update
items.detail: Keep improving them as new risks or weaknesses appear, guided by accepted security practice.

cards.title: May we use it at all? Grounds, minimality, purpose and retention
cards.body:
Before security even comes up, POPIA asks whether processing is allowed:

- **A valid ground (s 11):** consent; necessity for a contract with the person; a legal obligation (for example the bank's FIC Act customer due diligence); protecting the person's legitimate interest; a public law duty; or the legitimate interests of the bank or a third party. If the bank relies on consent, it must be able to prove it, and consent can be withdrawn.
- **Objection:** people may object on reasonable grounds to processing based on legitimate interests, and may object to direct marketing.
- **Minimality (s 10):** only information that is adequate, relevant and not excessive for the purpose.
- **Purpose (s 13):** a specific, explicitly defined and lawful purpose, made known to the person.
- **Retention (s 14):** keep records no longer than needed, unless the law, a contract, consent or a lawful need requires more; then destroy, delete or de-identify them so they cannot be reconstructed.
- **Further use (s 15):** later uses must be compatible with the original purpose.

cards.title: Which condition is in play?
cards.prompt: Match each Marula Bank situation to the POPIA condition it mainly tests.

pairs.left: Using account-opening data to target a credit card campaign
pairs.right: Further processing limitation: is the new use compatible with the original purpose?

pairs.left: Asking new customers for their religion 'just in case'
pairs.right: Processing limitation (minimality): it is not relevant or needed for a bank account

pairs.left: Keeping closed-account files forever 'to be safe'
pairs.right: Purpose specification (retention): keep only as long as needed or legally required

pairs.left: A customer asks what information the bank holds about him
pairs.right: Data subject participation: the right to access and ask for correction

pairs.left: A spreadsheet of applicants is emailed to a personal address
pairs.right: Security safeguards: integrity and confidentiality are compromised

lines.text: Next item: the document archiving firm in Midrand that scans and stores our loan files. Fatima, are we covered?
The contract is from 2015. It says nothing about security measures or about telling us if files are accessed by someone who shouldn't see them.
And they have remote access to our document system. Under the cyber standard that makes their staff users too.
Under POPIA they're our operator. The bank must have a written contract making sure they keep proper security, and they must tell us immediately if they suspect unauthorised access.

cards.title: Fixing the operator gap
cards.situation: Marula's archiving firm processes thousands of loan files containing ID numbers, payslips and bank statements. Its contract has no security or breach clauses. Procurement says renegotiating will take months and suggests 'just trusting them' because they have never had a problem.

choices.text: Accept procurement's view; a clean history is enough evidence of good security.
choices.outcome: Not enough. POPIA requires a written contract under which the operator keeps the security measures in section 19, and the operator must tell the bank immediately of suspected unauthorised access. History is not a control.

choices.text: Prioritise a contract amendment with security and immediate breach-notice terms, assess the firm's controls now, and record the risk and interim measures until it is signed.
choices.outcome: Best answer. It closes the legal gap, gives the bank evidence of the operator's safeguards, and manages the risk transparently in the meantime, which also supports Joint Standard 2's third-party requirements.

choices.text: Stop sending files to the archive firm and keep everything in branch storerooms.
choices.outcome: Moving files to storerooms can create new risks and does not fix the existing contract. Halting without a plan is not a safeguard.

choices.text: Email the firm asking it to confirm in writing that it follows POPIA.
choices.outcome: A step in the right direction, but a general confirmation is not a contract setting the security measures and breach notice, and it does not test the controls.

cards.title: Responsible party and operator: who does what

items.label: Who decides
items.left: Decides the purpose and means of processing
items.right: Processes for the bank under a contract or mandate

items.label: Authority
items.right: Acts only with the bank's knowledge or authorisation (s 20)

items.label: Security
items.left: Must ensure by written contract that the operator keeps s 19 measures (s 21)

items.label: Suspected breach
items.left: Notifies the Regulator and data subjects (s 22)

cards.title: Special personal information or not?
cards.prompt: POPIA gives extra protection to special personal information (s 26). Sort these.

items.text: A customer's medical condition mentioned in a hardship application
A fingerprint template used for biometric login
Details of a criminal charge against a loan applicant
A customer's religious beliefs
A customer's bank account number
A customer's email address and mobile number
A customer's monthly salary
A company client's registered address

cards.question: What is the most an administrative fine can be under section 109 of POPIA?
options: R1 million
R5 million
R10 million
R50 million
cards.explanation: Section 109 caps an administrative fine in an infringement notice at R10 million. Civil claims and criminal penalties are separate routes.

cards.title: Three POPIA habits for every desk
cards.body: **Ask why** before you collect or share: is there a purpose and a valid ground? **Share the minimum**: send only the fields the task needs, through approved channels, never to personal email or apps. **Lock and dispose**: lock screens, encrypt devices, and use approved destruction so records cannot be put back together.

cards.title: Story case: the overshared spreadsheet
cards.body:
*This is the quest's own fictional case.* A Marula credit analyst needed help from a colleague at the Durban hub with five problem loan files. To save time she emailed the whole month's applicant spreadsheet (2,300 rows with ID numbers, salaries and contact details) to the colleague's personal webmail because the bank's mail was slow.

**What went wrong under POPIA:**
- *Minimality and purpose:* five rows were needed; 2,300 were sent.
- *Security safeguards:* information left the bank's controlled systems for an uncontrolled account.
- *Accountability:* the bank cannot show who else may now see the data.

**What Marula did:** Fatima's team treated it as a possible security compromise, worked with the colleague to delete the copies and secure the webmail account, assessed whether there were reasonable grounds to believe anyone unauthorised had accessed the data, and recorded the decision. It then added data loss prevention rules and a coaching session for the team.

cards.title: Stage 3 take-aways
items: POPIA sets eight conditions for lawful processing; the bank, as responsible party, is accountable for all of them.
Processing needs a valid ground, a specific purpose, only relevant information and no longer retention than needed.
Section 19: identify risks, build safeguards, verify them regularly and keep them updated.
Operators need a written contract with security measures and must tell the bank immediately of suspected unauthorised access.
Special personal information gets extra protection; administrative fines can reach R10 million.

cards.prompt: Pick one task you do that involves customer information. What is its purpose, which fields do you really need, where does the information travel, and how is it destroyed when the task is done?

quiz.question: Under POPIA, what is the bank when it decides why and how customer information is processed?
options: The operator
The data subject
The responsible party
The information regulator
quiz.explanation: A responsible party decides the purpose of and means for processing. An operator processes for it under a contract or mandate.

quiz.question: How many conditions for the lawful processing of personal information does section 4 of POPIA list?
options: Five
Six
Eight
Ten
quiz.explanation: Section 4 lists eight conditions: accountability, processing limitation, purpose specification, further processing limitation, information quality, openness, security safeguards and data subject participation.

quiz.question: Marketing wants to use income data collected at account opening to target customers for a new credit card. Which POPIA condition must be assessed first?
options: Further processing limitation: is the new use compatible with the original purpose?
Openness: is the bank's PAIA manual up to date?
Information quality: is the income figure still accurate?
Data subject participation: has anyone asked for access?
quiz.explanation: Section 15 requires further processing to be compatible with the purpose of collection, taking into account factors such as the relationship between purposes and the consequences for the person.

quiz.question: Which of these is part of the section 19 duty to secure personal information?
options: Publishing customers' details to prove transparency
Regularly verifying that safeguards are effectively implemented
Keeping every record permanently
Letting operators set their own security rules
quiz.explanation: Section 19 requires the responsible party to identify foreseeable risks, set up safeguards, regularly verify that they work and keep them updated.

quiz.question: A cloud provider processing Marula Bank's customer data suspects an intruder accessed it. Under POPIA, what must the provider do?
options: Notify only the Information Regulator, not the bank
Wait until the investigation is complete
Notify the bank immediately
Notify the affected customers directly instead of the bank
quiz.explanation: Section 21(2) requires an operator to notify the responsible party immediately when there are reasonable grounds to believe information was accessed or acquired by an unauthorised person.

quiz.question: Which of these is special personal information under section 26 of POPIA?
options: A customer's email address
A company's registered address
A customer's account balance
Biometric information such as a fingerprint template
quiz.explanation: Special personal information includes religious or philosophical beliefs, race or ethnic origin, trade union membership, political persuasion, health or sex life, biometric information and certain criminal behaviour information.

quiz.question: A bank relies on a customer's consent to process information for an optional rewards programme. Who must prove the consent was given?
options: The customer
The Information Regulator
The bank, as responsible party
The rewards partner only
quiz.explanation: Section 11(2) places the burden of proof for consent on the responsible party. The person may also withdraw consent at any time.

quiz.question: What does POPIA require when a record of personal information no longer needs to be kept?
options: Move it to an archive indefinitely
Send it back to the Regulator
Keep it for marketing use
Destroy, delete or de-identify it so it cannot be reconstructed
quiz.explanation: Section 14 requires destruction, deletion or de-identification as soon as reasonably practicable once retention is no longer authorised, in a way that prevents reconstruction.

quiz.question: Who must be registered with the Information Regulator before taking up their POPIA duties?
options: Every employee who handles customer data
The information officer
Every operator's staff member
Each data subject
quiz.explanation: Section 55(2) says information officers may take up their duties only after the responsible party has registered them with the Regulator.

quiz.question: A customer sues the bank for damages after a POPIA breach. The bank argues it did not act intentionally or negligently. Under section 99, is that a complete answer?
options: Yes: intent must always be proved
No: liability can arise whether or not there was intent or negligence
Yes: only the Regulator can sue
No: but only criminal courts may hear it
quiz.explanation: Section 99 allows a civil action for damages whether or not there is intent or negligence. The Act lists specific defences, such as vis major or that compliance was not reasonably practicable.

sessions.title: Incidents: Detect, Respond and Notify
sessions.summary: Detecting and responding to cyber incidents under Joint Standard 2, deciding when an incident is material, notifying the PA under Joint Notice 2 of 2026, and notifying the Information Regulator and customers under POPIA section 22.
objectives: Distinguish cyber events, cyber incidents and material incidents as Joint Standard 2 defines them
Describe the incident response plan the standard requires and your own escalation role
Apply the Joint Notice 2 of 2026 template timelines and filing route for banks
Apply POPIA sections 21 and 22 on operator notice, notification to the Regulator and customers, and allowed delay

cards.title: 02:10 on a Friday
cards.setting: Security operations centre, Midrand. Early Friday morning, with a video link to the Durban hub.

lines.text: We have encryption spreading on two file servers at the Durban hub. One holds scanned loan applications. I've isolated the network segment.
Good. Start the incident response plan. First questions: what's affected, are customer services down, and has anything left the building?
Branch systems in KwaZulu-Natal can't open loan files. Core banking is fine so far. We see a large outbound transfer from one server last night.
If loan files went out, we may have personal information in the hands of criminals. That's POPIA section 22 territory.
And if we classify this as material, the Joint Notice clock starts for the Prudential Authority. Two regimes, one incident. Welcome to stage four.

scenes.heading: Events
scenes.narration: IT systems produce countless events. Joint Standard 2 expects banks to monitor them, through a security operations centre or managed security service, and to escalate anything suspicious quickly.

scenes.heading: Incidents
scenes.narration: An event becomes a cyber incident when it threatens the security of a system or its information, or breaks security or acceptable use policy.

scenes.heading: Material incidents
scenes.narration: An incident is material when it has, or is likely to have, a severe and widespread impact on the bank's operations, its customers, or the wider financial system and economy.

scenes.heading: The plan
scenes.narration: The bank must have a tested incident response and management plan that isolates and neutralises the incident, resumes services securely, investigates root causes and feeds lessons back.

scenes.heading: Classification triggers notice
scenes.narration: Once the bank classifies a cyber incident or information security compromise as material, it must notify the responsible authority in the form the authorities set.

items.label: Detect and escalate
items.detail: Monitoring or a staff report raises the alarm; escalate to the incident team at once.

items.label: Triage and classify
items.detail: Assess scope and impact against the bank's materiality criteria.

items.label: Contain
items.detail: Isolate affected systems and accounts to stop the spread.

items.label: Recover
items.detail: Restore from secure backups within recovery objectives; keep customers informed.

items.label: Notify
items.detail: Regulators, the Information Regulator and customers, as each rule requires.

items.label: Learn
items.detail: Find the control gaps, fix them and update the plan and training.

cards.question: Under Joint Standard 2, what makes an incident 'material'?
options: Any incident that involves a virus
A severe and widespread impact, actual or likely, on operations, customers or the wider financial system
Any incident lasting longer than one hour
Any incident reported in the media
cards.explanation: The standard defines a material incident by its actual or likely severe and widespread impact on the institution's operations, its customers, or the broader financial system and economy.

cards.title: Joint Notice 2 of 2026: the notification template clock
cards.caption: Timelines as set out in the instructions of the Reporting of Material IT and Cyber Incident Template (Annexure A). Check the current template before filing.

items.label: Immediate notification
items.detail: Within 24 hours after classifying the incident as material: contact details and incident details, plus cyber details for a cyber incident.

items.label: Subsequent update
items.detail: Within 14 calendar days from the notification: the impact of the incident.

items.label: Full incident report
items.detail: On timelines agreed with the authority: all parts of the template and the final investigation report.

items.label: In force
items.detail: The determination of the template took effect on this date.

cards.title: What Joint Notice 2 of 2026 changed
cards.body:
The PA and FSCA signed **Joint Notice 2 of 2026** on 31 August 2026. It sets the form, manner and period for notifying **material IT and cyber incidents** under paragraph 15.1 of Joint Standard 1 and paragraph 9.1 of Joint Standard 2, and took effect on **1 September 2026**.

- **Form:** the 'Reporting of Material IT and Cyber Incident Template', attached as Annexure A.
- **Manner for banks:** banks, branches of foreign banks, controlling companies and mutual banks complete and submit the template on the PA's secure **Umoja portal** as a notification. Other institutions, such as fund managers, use the FSCA's Joint Standards Submission Portal.
- **Period:** set out on the template's cover page (see the clock above).

The template asks for much more than 'what broke': detection time, attack type (phishing, vishing, ransomware and others), whether customer data was leaked, how customers were told and supported, whether the incident went to the board, whether other authorities such as the **Information Regulator** were told, root cause and lessons learnt. Good records from minute one make it possible to answer.

cards.title: Which notification route?
cards.prompt: For each fact in the Durban incident, which route does it mainly trigger?

items.text: Branch loan systems across a province are down for days, with severe impact
Reasonable grounds to believe an attacker copied customer ID numbers and payslips
A material ransomware incident in which customer files were also stolen
Core banking outage classified as material, with no personal information touched
A small, contained leak of 40 customers' details by email to a stranger
A widespread system failure after a faulty update, classified as material

cards.title: Who do we tell, and when?

lines.text: I've been told the board must hear about this. What are we telling the regulators, and when?
We classified it as material at 08:00 given the regional outage. The Umoja notification is due within 24 hours of that, and an impact update within 14 days.

Forensics confirms loan files were copied. So there are reasonable grounds to believe personal information was acquired by an unauthorised person. POPIA says we must notify the Regulator and the customers as soon as reasonably possible.
The police want a few days before we tell customers. They're tracing the attackers.
POPIA allows a delay to customers only if a public body investigating offences, or the Regulator, decides notice would impede a criminal investigation. Let's get that in writing.

cards.title: The notification call
cards.situation: It is Friday morning. The Durban incident has been classified as material. Forensics shows that files with about 3,000 customers' ID numbers and payslips were copied out. The marketing head says: 'Let's wait until we know everything before telling anyone. We don't want headlines.'

choices.text: Agree to wait until the full investigation ends, then report once with all the facts.
choices.outcome: Wrong on both counts. The PA notification is due within 24 hours of classification, with updates later; and POPIA requires notice as soon as reasonably possible after discovery. Waiting for perfect facts breaks both.

choices.text: File the PA notification on Umoja within 24 hours of classification, notify the Information Regulator and affected customers as soon as reasonably possible, and record any written law enforcement request to delay customer notice.
choices.outcome: Best answer. Each regime is met on its own terms. Section 22 lets the bank take account of law enforcement needs and scoping, and allows delaying customer notice only when a public body or the Regulator decides it would impede a criminal investigation.

choices.text: Notify the Information Regulator only; the PA does not need to know about data theft.
choices.outcome: Incomplete. The incident is classified as material, so Joint Standard 2 and the Joint Notice require notice to the PA as well. The template even asks whether other authorities were told.

choices.text: Notify the PA now and tell customers only if the stolen data appears online.
choices.outcome: Half right. The PA notice is correct, but POPIA's trigger is reasonable grounds to believe personal information was accessed or acquired, not proof that it was published.

cards.title: Two notification regimes side by side

items.label: Rule
items.left: Joint Standard 2 para 9.1 and Joint Notice 2 of 2026

items.label: Trigger
items.left: Bank classifies a cyber incident or compromise as material
items.right: Reasonable grounds to believe personal information was accessed or acquired without authority

items.label: Who is told
items.left: The responsible authority (for banks, the PA via Umoja)
items.right: The Information Regulator and the affected data subjects

items.label: When
items.left: Within 24 hours of classification, update within 14 days, then full report
items.right: As soon as reasonably possible after discovery

items.label: Allowed delay
items.left: None stated beyond the template timelines
items.right: Customer notice only if law enforcement or the Regulator says it would impede an investigation

cards.back: In writing: by post to the last known address, by email, by a prominent notice on the bank's website, through the news media, or as the Regulator directs.
Possible consequences, what the bank has done or will do, what the customer can do to protect themselves, and the identity of the unauthorised person if known.

cards.front: What if the customer can't be identified?
cards.back: The duty to notify the data subject applies unless the person's identity cannot be established; the Regulator must still be told.
Yes. If it believes publicity would protect affected people, it may direct the bank to publicise the compromise.

cards.front: What may the bank take into account on timing?
cards.back: Legitimate law enforcement needs and the steps reasonably needed to find the scope and restore system integrity.

cards.question: An operator tells Marula Bank that it suspects someone accessed the bank's customer data. Who must notify the Information Regulator and the affected customers under POPIA?
options: The operator, because it held the data
The bank, as responsible party
The police
Nobody until the attacker is identified
cards.explanation: The operator must tell the bank immediately (s 21). The bank, as responsible party, must notify the Regulator and the data subjects under section 22.

cards.title: Real case: how the Justice department handled its 2021 ransomware attack
cards.body:
After ransomware struck on 6 September 2021, the Department of Justice and Constitutional Development published updates on gov.za. Its first statement said it had **activated its business continuity plan**, used manual recording so courts could keep sitting, issued documents to bereaved families by hand, and was working with state agencies. At that point it said no data compromise had been detected.

By 10 October 2021 the picture had moved on. The department reported that the malware had been contained and services were being restored step by step. After a high-level assessment of a **possible leak of personal information**, and in line with POPIA, it **issued a notice on its website to its data subjects**. It also said it had upgraded its ICT security infrastructure and tightened electronic and physical access control.

**Lessons:** a first assessment can change; keep re-assessing whether personal information was reached. A website notice is one of the channels section 22 allows. And the fixes it named (security tooling and access control) are exactly the controls Joint Standard 2 expects before an attack.

*Sources: department statements on gov.za, 20 September and 10 October 2021.*

cards.title: Stage 4 take-aways
items: Joint Standard 2 requires monitoring, escalation and a tested incident response plan that isolates, recovers, investigates and learns.
A material incident has, or is likely to have, a severe and widespread impact on operations, customers or the financial system.
From 1 September 2026 banks notify material IT and cyber incidents on the Umoja portal: within 24 hours of classification, an update within 14 days, then a full report.
POPIA s 22: notify the Information Regulator and affected people as soon as reasonably possible when there are reasonable grounds to believe information was accessed or acquired.
One incident can trigger both regimes. Keep records from the first minute.

cards.prompt: If you noticed something odd on your screen tonight, who exactly would you call, and what three facts would you write down first so the incident team could classify it quickly?

quiz.question: From 1 September 2026, where does a South African bank submit the template for a material IT or cyber incident?
options: By email to the Information Regulator
On the FSCA's complaints portal
Through the Financial Intelligence Centre's reporting system
On the Prudential Authority's Umoja portal
quiz.explanation: Joint Notice 2 of 2026 requires banks, branches, controlling companies and mutual banks to complete and submit the template on the PA's Umoja portal.

quiz.question: Under the template instructions, when is the immediate notification of a material cyber incident due?
options: Within 24 hours after the incident is classified as material
Within 72 hours after the incident started
Within 14 calendar days after detection
Only after the final investigation report
quiz.explanation: The template's instructions set immediate notification within 24 hours following classification as material. The impact update follows within 14 calendar days of notification.

quiz.question: What is the trigger for a POPIA section 22 notification?
options: Proof that stolen data has been published online
Reasonable grounds to believe personal information was accessed or acquired by an unauthorised person
A system outage of more than one day
A complaint from at least ten customers
quiz.explanation: Section 22(1) is triggered by reasonable grounds to believe personal information has been accessed or acquired by an unauthorised person.

quiz.question: Which of these is an allowed channel for notifying a customer under section 22(4)?
options: A verbal message to the customer's neighbour
A post on a staff WhatsApp group
An entry in the bank's internal risk register
A prominent notice on the bank's website
quiz.explanation: Section 22(4) allows written notice by post, email, a prominent website notice, the news media or as the Regulator directs.

quiz.question: When may a bank delay notifying affected customers of a compromise under POPIA?
options: Whenever the bank fears media coverage
When a public body investigating offences or the Regulator decides notice would impede a criminal investigation
Until the bank's share price recovers
Until the end of the financial year
quiz.explanation: Section 22(3) allows delaying notice to data subjects only if such a public body or the Regulator determines that notification will impede a criminal investigation.

quiz.question: What must the subsequent update under the template, due within 14 calendar days of notification, mainly cover?
options: The bank's annual financial statements
The impact of the incident
The names of all staff on duty
The bank's marketing plan for affected customers
quiz.explanation: The template instructions link the subsequent update to the tab on the impact of the incident; the full report later includes all tabs and the final investigation report.

quiz.question: Which element must Joint Standard 2's incident response and management plan include?
options: A promise never to inform customers
A rule that only the CEO may respond
A ban on involving third parties
A process to investigate the control gaps that led to the compromise
quiz.explanation: The plan must isolate and neutralise incidents, resume services securely, investigate the control deficiencies and full impact, feed in lessons learnt and be tested.

quiz.question: A faulty software update causes a nationwide card outage that the bank classifies as material. No personal information is involved. Which notification applies?
options: Notification to the PA under the Joint Standards template
Notification to the Information Regulator under POPIA s 22
No notification, because there was no attack
Notification to customers only
quiz.explanation: Joint Standard 1 paragraph 15.1 covers material IT incidents such as failures and malfunctions, and Joint Notice 2 of 2026 applies the template. POPIA s 22 needs unauthorised access to personal information.

quiz.question: What must a POPIA section 22 notice to a customer include?
options: The bank's internal incident ticket number only
A waiver of the customer's right to claim damages
The names of the staff involved
A recommendation on steps the customer can take to reduce the possible harm
quiz.explanation: Section 22(5) requires the possible consequences, the bank's measures, recommendations for the customer's own protective steps, and the attacker's identity if known.

quiz.question: Which Joint Standard 2 requirement deals with keeping customers informed during a cyber attack?
options: A clear communication strategy for affected customers, including the recourse available
A rule that customers must sign a non-disclosure agreement
A ban on any customer communication until the attack ends
A requirement to publish all forensic reports
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 7.4.1 requires a clear communication strategy for financial customers affected by cyber attacks, including details of any recourse available.

sessions.title: Operational Resilience, Testing and Assessment Readiness
sessions.summary: PA Directive 4 of 2023 and the Basel resilience principles, how Joint Standards 1 and 2 and POPIA fit together, Joint Standard 2's testing and remediation cycles, roles across the bank, and the evidence a supervisor expects to see.
objectives: Explain what Directive 4 of 2023 requires and the seven categories of the Basel resilience principles
Show how Directive 4, Joint Standards 1 and 2 and POPIA fit together
Apply Joint Standard 2's testing, simulation and remediation requirements and review cycles
Prepare evidence of training, testing and board oversight for a supervisory review

cards.title: Four weeks to the review
cards.setting: Board room, Marula Bank head office, Rosebank. A Thursday in late November.

lines.text: The PA review is in four weeks. They want our cyber programme, our training evidence and how we meet the operational resilience directive. Where do we stand?
The Durban incident hurt, but it showed our plan works. Systems recovered within our objectives and we filed on Umoja on time.
Our last simulation exercise was a table-top. The standard wants scenario exercises that include an adversarial attack and defence. We haven't done that yet.
And the contact centre partner's agents finished the yearly refresher. I have the completion records.
We should also show the board how POPIA, the Joint Standards and the resilience directive fit together. One picture, not four binders.
Then that's stage five: the Resilience Summit. Let's get ready to show, not just tell.

scenes.heading: The source
scenes.narration: In March 2021 the Basel Committee published principles for operational resilience. The Prudential Authority adopted them for South African banks through a directive under the Banks Act.

scenes.heading: Replacing the old directive
scenes.narration: Directive 4 of 2023, dated 1 June 2023, replaced Directive 10 of 2021 and moved the compliance date to 31 December 2024 to align with other countries.

scenes.heading: Part of risk management
scenes.narration: Operational resilience must be built into the bank's enterprise risk management and board-approved policies, as the Banks Act regulations on governance require. It applies on a consolidated, group basis.

scenes.heading: Risk-based and harmonised
scenes.narration: Banks must assess their policies and practices against the principles, apply them in line with risk appetite, run business continuity and third-party management consistently, and align with critical functions in recovery and resolution plans.

scenes.heading: Teeth
scenes.narration: If the PA judges a bank's resilience policies inadequate, the regulations let it require the bank to hold extra capital or to align its policies with its risk exposure.

cards.title: The seven categories of resilience principles

cards.back: The board approves and oversees the resilience approach, including tolerance for disruption.
Identify and manage operational risks and keep controls effective.
Plans that keep critical operations running through severe but plausible disruption, tested regularly.
Know the people, technology, processes, information and facilities that critical operations depend on.
Manage the risk from service providers and other third parties that critical operations rely on.
Find, record, respond to, recover from and learn from incidents.
Technology and cyber controls that protect and restore critical operations.

cards.question: By what date did Directive 4 of 2023 require banks to comply with the operational resilience requirements?
options: 30 June 2023
31 December 2024
1 June 2025
1 September 2026
cards.explanation: Directive 4 of 2023 replaced Directive 10 of 2021, which had effectively set 30 June 2023, and required compliance on or before 31 December 2024.

cards.title: How the rulebook fits together
cards.body:
Four instruments, one aim: a bank that keeps serving customers safely through disruption.

- **Directive 4 of 2023 (PA, Banks Act):** the umbrella. Operational resilience across governance, risk, continuity, mapping, third parties, incidents and ICT.
- **Joint Standard 1 of 2023 (PA and FSCA):** IT governance and risk management.
